content: Gum disease, also known as gingivitis, refers to the inflammation of the gums, or gingiva. Symptoms of Gum Disease: The gums may appear bright red or have a red-purple discoloration. The gums may feel tender to the touch, although they are typically not painful otherwise. Mouth sores may develop. Swelling of the gums is common. The gums may have a shiny or glossy appearance. Causes of Gum Disease: Gingivitis is a type of periodontal disease, which involves inflammation and infection that damages the tissues supporting the teeth, including the gums, periodontal ligaments, and alveolar bone (tooth sockets). The primary cause of gingivitis is the prolonged accumulation of plaque, a sticky substance composed of bacteria, mucus, and food particles that forms on the exposed surfaces of teeth. If plaque is not removed, it hardens into tartar, which becomes lodged at the base of the teeth. Both plaque and tartar irritate the gums, leading to inflammation. Bacteria and their toxins further contribute to infection, swelling, and tenderness of the gums. Overly aggressive brushing or flossing can also injure the gums and trigger gingivitis. Risk factors for gingivitis include: General illnesses that weaken the immune system. Poor oral hygiene practices. Hormonal changes during pregnancy, which increase gum sensitivity. Uncontrolled diabetes. Misaligned teeth, rough dental fillings, or poorly maintained dental appliances (e.g., braces, dentures, bridges, crowns) that irritate the gums. High-Risk Groups: Gingivitis is common and can affect individuals to varying degrees. It often begins during puberty or early adulthood due to hormonal changes. The condition may persist or recur depending on the overall health of the teeth and gums. Diagnosis: A dentist will assess the mouth and teeth, looking for signs such as soft, swollen, or red-purple gums. Plaque and tartar deposits may be visible at the base of the teeth. The gums are typically painless or only mildly tender. When to Seek Medical Attention: You should contact your dentist if you notice symptoms of gingivitis, particularly if you have not had a professional cleaning or dental examination in the past six months. If your dentist identifies underlying conditions contributing to gingivitis, you may need to consult a healthcare provider for further treatment. Treatment Options: The primary goal of treatment is to reduce gum inflammation. A dentist or dental hygienist will perform a thorough cleaning to remove plaque and tartar deposits. This may involve the use of specialized instruments or devices. After professional cleaning, maintaining proper oral hygiene is essential. Dentists or hygienists will provide guidance on effective brushing and flossing techniques. In severe cases, professional cleanings may be recommended more frequently, such as twice a year or more. Antibacterial mouth rinses or other aids may be prescribed to complement brushing and flossing. Any underlying medical conditions that exacerbate gingivitis should also be addressed. Prognosis: The removal of plaque from inflamed gums may cause some discomfort. However, symptoms such as bleeding and tenderness typically improve within one to two weeks following professional cleaning and consistent oral hygiene. Warm saltwater rinses or antibacterial mouthwashes can help reduce gum swelling, while over-the-counter anti-inflammatory medications can alleviate discomfort from intensive cleaning. Healthy gums should appear pink and firm. Lifelong adherence to strict oral hygiene practices is necessary to prevent the recurrence of gingivitis. Potential Complications: Recurrence of gingivitis. Progression to periodontitis, a more severe form of gum disease. Development of infections or abscesses in the gums or jawbones. Trench mouth, a severe and painful form of gum infection. Prevention: The most effective way to prevent gingivitis is through good oral hygiene, which removes the plaque responsible for the condition. Brush your teeth at least twice daily and floss gently at least once a day. For individuals prone to gingivitis, brushing and flossing after every meal and before bedtime may be recommended. Seek guidance from a dentist or dental hygienist on proper brushing and flossing techniques. Special tools, such as interdental brushes, water flossers, or antiplaque toothpastes and mouth rinses, may be suggested for individuals with a high risk of plaque buildup. Regular professional cleanings, typically every six months, are crucial for removing plaque that may accumulate despite diligent oral hygiene.
